title: Erie R.R. v. Tompkins, 304 U.S. 64 (1938)
court: Supreme Court of the United States
content:
Erie R.R. v. Tompkins, 304 U.S. 64 (1938).

[Excerpt — holding summary, not copyrighted headnotes.]

The Supreme Court held that except in matters governed by the Federal Constitution or by Acts of Congress, the law to be applied in any case is the law of the state. There is no federal general common law. Federal courts sitting in diversity must apply state substantive law as declared by the state's highest court.

opinionParts.content: Except in matters governed by the Federal Constitution or by Acts of Congress, the law to be applied in any case is the law of the state. There is no federal general common law.

title: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
court: Supreme Court of the United States
content:
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007).

[Excerpt — holding summary, not copyrighted headnotes.]

The Court held that a complaint must contain sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face. Threadbare recitals of the elements of a cause of action, supported by mere conclusory statements, do not suffice.

opinionParts.content: A complaint must contain sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.

title: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
court: Supreme Court of the United States
content:
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009).

[Excerpt — holding summary, not copyrighted headnotes.]

The Court reaffirmed Twombly's plausibility standard and held that courts must accept all well-pleaded factual allegations as true but need not accept legal conclusions cast as factual allegations. When ruling on a motion to dismiss, courts must draw on their experience and common sense.

opinionParts.content: Courts must accept all well-pleaded factual allegations as true but need not accept legal conclusions cast as factual allegations. The plausibility standard governs Rule 12(b)(6) review.

title: Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)
court: Supreme Court of the United States
content:
Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986).

[Excerpt — holding summary, not copyrighted headnotes.]

The Court held that under Rule 56, the party moving for summary judgment bears the initial responsibility of informing the district court of the basis for its motion and identifying portions of the record demonstrating the absence of a genuine issue of material fact.

opinionParts.content: The party moving for summary judgment bears the initial responsibility of informing the district court of the basis for its motion and identifying portions of the record demonstrating the absence of a genuine issue of material fact.

title: Chevron U.S.A. Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc., 467 U.S. 837 (1984)
court: Supreme Court of the United States
content:
Chevron U.S.A. Inc. v. NRDC, 467 U.S. 837 (1984).

[Excerpt — holding summary, not copyrighted headnotes.]

The Court held that when a statute is silent or ambiguous on the specific issue, the question for the court is whether the agency's answer is based on a permissible construction of the statute. If Congress has explicitly left a gap, that gap may be filled by reasonable agency interpretation entitled to deference.

opinionParts.content: When a statute is silent or ambiguous on the specific issue, courts ask whether the agency's answer is based on a permissible construction of the statute.

sourceMetadata.excerptNote: Historical holding excerpt; subsequent treatment altered by Loper Bright (2024).

title: Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024)
court: Supreme Court of the United States
content:
Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024).

[Excerpt — holding summary, not copyrighted headnotes.]

The Supreme Court overruled Chevron and held that the Administrative Procedure Act requires courts to exercise independent judgment in deciding whether an agency has acted within its statutory authority. Courts may not defer to an agency interpretation of a statute simply because a statute is ambiguous.

opinionParts.content: Courts must exercise their independent judgment in deciding whether an agency has acted within its statutory authority. Chevron is overruled.

title: Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 436 (1966)
court: Supreme Court of the United States
content:
Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 436 (1966).

[Excerpt — holding summary, not copyrighted headnotes.]

The Court held that the prosecution may not use statements stemming from custodial interrogation of the defendant unless it demonstrates the use of procedural safeguards effective to secure the privilege against self-incrimination. Prior to questioning, the person must be warned that he has a right to remain silent and that anything said can be used against him.

opinionParts.content: The prosecution may not use statements stemming from custodial interrogation unless procedural safeguards effective to secure the privilege against self-incrimination were employed.

title: Gideon v. Wainwright, 372 U.S. 335 (1963)
court: Supreme Court of the United States
content:
Gideon v. Wainwright, 372 U.S. 335 (1963).

[Excerpt — holding summary, not copyrighted headnotes.]

The Court held that the Sixth Amendment right to counsel is a fundamental right essential to a fair trial, and that the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment makes that right obligatory upon the States. States must provide counsel to defendants unable to afford an attorney in felony cases.

opinionParts.content: The right to counsel is a fundamental right, and the Fourteenth Amendment makes the Sixth Amendment's guarantee of counsel obligatory upon the States.

title: International Shoe Co. v. Washington, 326 U.S. 310 (1945)
court: Supreme Court of the United States
content:
International Shoe Co. v. Washington, 326 U.S. 310 (1945).

[Excerpt — holding summary, not copyrighted headnotes.]

The Court held that due process requires only that a defendant have such minimum contacts with the forum that maintenance of the suit does not offend traditional notions of fair play and substantial justice. Personal jurisdiction depends on the quality and nature of the defendant's activity in relation to the forum.

opinionParts.content: Due process requires only that a defendant have such minimum contacts with the forum that maintenance of the suit does not offend traditional notions of fair play and substantial justice.

title: Hertz Corp. v. Friend, 559 U.S. 77 (2010)
court: Supreme Court of the United States
content:
Hertz Corp. v. Friend, 559 U.S. 77 (2010).

[Excerpt — holding summary, not copyrighted headnotes.]

The Court held that a corporation's principal place of business for diversity jurisdiction purposes refers to the place where the corporation's high-level officers direct, control, and coordinate the corporation's activities, which courts have called the corporation's nerve center, typically its headquarters.

opinionParts.content: A corporation's principal place of business refers to the place where its high-level officers direct, control, and coordinate activities — the nerve center, typically its headquarters.

title: United States v. Microsoft Corp., 253 F.3d 34 (D.C. Cir. 2001)
court: United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit
content:
United States v. Microsoft Corp., 253 F.3d 34 (D.C. Cir. 2001).

[Excerpt — holding summary, not copyrighted headnotes.]

The D.C. Circuit affirmed in part and reversed in part a district court judgment finding Microsoft liable for monopolization and attempted monopolization under Section 2 of the Sherman Act. The court held that Microsoft's actions taken to protect its operating-system monopoly were exclusionary and violated Section 2, while remanding on remedy issues.

opinionParts.content: Microsoft's actions taken to protect its operating-system monopoly were exclusionary and violated Section 2 of the Sherman Act.

title: In re Facebook, Inc. IPO Securities & ERISA Litigation, 821 F.3d 633 (9th Cir. 2016)
court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
content:
In re Facebook, Inc. IPO Securities & ERISA Litigation, 821 F.3d 633 (9th Cir. 2016).

[Excerpt — holding summary, not copyrighted headnotes.]

The Ninth Circuit addressed securities fraud claims arising from Facebook's initial public offering and held that plaintiffs must plead loss causation with particularity under the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act when alleging that defendants' misrepresentations caused economic loss.

opinionParts.content: Plaintiffs must plead loss causation with particularity under the PSLRA when alleging that misrepresentations caused economic loss in securities fraud claims.

title: Harper v. Deposition Corp. of America, 954 F.2d 1140 (6th Cir. 1992)
court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
content:
Harper v. Deposition Corp. of America, 954 F.2d 1140 (6th Cir. 1992).

[Excerpt — holding summary, not copyrighted headnotes.]

The Sixth Circuit addressed summary judgment standards and held that the moving party may satisfy its burden by demonstrating that there is an absence of evidence to support the nonmoving party's case, consistent with Celotex.

opinionParts.content: The moving party may satisfy its summary judgment burden by demonstrating that there is an absence of evidence to support the nonmoving party's case.
